items.stem: A force of 50 N pulls a sledge 20 m along level snow; the rope is at 30° to the horizontal. What work does the force do?
A teacher in Oslo asks a class to choose the one correct statement about work done by a force and the work-energy principle. Which statement should be chosen?
options: Energy is used up when a ball rolls to a stop.
A heavier object dropped from the same height lands with greater speed.
Only the component of force along the displacement does work; a centripetal force, for example, is perpendicular to the motion and does no work.
An efficient machine produces more energy than it receives.
items.answer: Only the component of force along the displacement does work; a centripetal force, for example, is perpendicular to the motion and does no work.
items.markingKey: C. The other options are common misconceptions. Only the component of force along the displacement does work; a centripetal force, for example, is perpendicular to the motion and does no work.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the force itself and work done by a force.
items.answer: A force is a vector push or pull (N); work is the scalar energy transferred when the force moves through a displacement along its direction (J). A large force does no work if there is no displacement.
items.markingKey: A force is a vector push or pull (N); work is the scalar energy transferred when the force moves through a displacement along its direction (J). A large force does no work if there is no displacement. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: The force on an archer’s arrow rises linearly from 0 to 200 N over the first 0.2 m and then linearly to 500 N over the next 0.10 m. Calculate the work done on the arrow.
A 1500 kg car travelling at 25 m s⁻¹ stops in 60 m. Use the work–energy principle to calculate the average braking force.
Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The work–energy principle makes Newton’s second law unnecessary."
items.answer: The two approaches complement each other: energy methods are convenient when time is not needed, but Newton’s laws are more fundamental and give more detail.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it solves many problems faster (no time or directions needed); it handles varying forces via the area under graphs. Arguments against: it gives no information about time or direction of motion; it is itself derived from Newton’s second law; friction and internal energy must be accounted for carefully. Supported judgement: The two approaches complement each other: energy methods are convenient when time is not needed, but Newton’s laws are more fundamental and give more detail.

items.stem: No work is done on an object when the force is
items.answer: perpendicular to the displacement

items.stem: A satellite moves in a circular orbit at constant speed. The work done on it by gravity in one orbit is
items.answer: zero
items.markingKey: C. Gravity is perpendicular to the velocity.

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "Any force acting on a moving object does work on it." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Only the component of force along the displacement does work; a centripetal force, for example, is perpendicular to the motion and does no work.
items.markingKey: Only the component of force along the displacement does work; a centripetal force, for example, is perpendicular to the motion and does no work. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why a person carrying a heavy bag horizontally at constant velocity does no work on the bag against gravity.
items.answer: The force from the person is vertical (balancing the weight) while the displacement is horizontal; the angle is 90°, so W = Fs cos 90° = 0.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The force from the person is vertical (balancing the weight) while the displacement is horizontal; the angle is 90°, so W = Fs cos 90° = 0. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Maya writes: "Holding a heavy object still is hard work, so a lot of work is done on it." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Muscles use chemical energy (internal processes) but no work is done on the object because it does not move.
items.markingKey: Muscles use chemical energy (internal processes) but no work is done on the object because it does not move. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A crane in Dubai lifts a 2.0 kg load vertically at constant speed through 4.5 m. Calculate the work done by the crane on the load.
items.markingKey: At constant speed F = mg (M1); W = mgh = 88.3 J (A1).

items.stem: A 1800 kg car travelling at 25 m s⁻¹ stops in 40 m. Use the work–energy principle to calculate the average braking force.

A 25 kg suitcase is pulled 40 m across an airport floor by a strap at 35° to the horizontal with a tension of 80 N. The friction force is 50 N. (a) Calculate the work done by the tension. (b) Calculate the work done against friction. (c) Determine the final speed if it starts from rest. (d) Explain why the friction force would be smaller if the strap were steeper.
items.answer: (a) 80 × 40 × cos 35° = 2620 J; (b) 2000 J; (c) ½ × 25v² = 620 J, v = 7.04 m s⁻¹; (d) a steeper strap has a larger upward component, reducing the normal force and so the friction μN.
items.markingKey: (a) 80 × 40 × cos 35° = 2620 J; (b) 2000 J; (c) ½ × 25v² = 620 J, v = 7.04 m s⁻¹; (d) a steeper strap has a larger upward component, reducing the normal force and so the friction μN.

items.stem:
This question is about work done by a force and the work-energy principle.

(a) A 1200 kg car travelling at 25 m s⁻¹ stops in 50 m. Use the work–energy principle to calculate the average braking force. [2]

(b) With the help of a specific example, explain how the work done in stretching a spring can be found from a force–extension graph. [3]

(c) Outline one argument for and one against the statement: "The work–energy principle makes Newton’s second law unnecessary." [6]
items.answer: (a) 7500 N (b) Work is the area under the force–displacement graph; for a spring obeying Hooke’s law it is a triangle of area ½Fx = ½kx². (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) The two approaches complement each other: energy methods are convenient when time is not needed, but Newton’s laws are more fundamental and give more detail.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Fs = ½mv² (M1); F = ½ × 1200 × 25²/50 = 7500 N (A1). (b) [3 marks] Work is the area under the force–displacement graph; for a spring obeying Hooke’s law it is a triangle of area ½Fx = ½kx². (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) [6 marks] For: it solves many problems faster (no time or directions needed); it handles varying forces via the area under graphs. Against: it gives no information about time or direction of motion; it is itself derived from Newton’s second law; friction and internal energy must be accounted for carefully. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: The two approaches complement each other: energy methods are convenient when time is not needed, but Newton’s laws are more fundamental and give more detail.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "mechanical energy"?
options: The work done by the force
The ratio of useful output energy (or power) to total input energy (or power)
The energy stored in a deformed elastic object, E = ½kx² for a spring obeying Hooke’s law
The sum of the kinetic and potential energies of a system
items.answer: The sum of the kinetic and potential energies of a system
items.markingKey: D. "mechanical energy" is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of a system.

items.stem: Two balls of different mass are released from the same height on frictionless ramps of different shapes. At the bottom they have the same
items.answer: speed
items.markingKey: D. v = √(2gh) independent of mass and path.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the speed of a pendulum bob at the bottom of its swing does not depend on its mass.
items.answer: Loss of GPE mgh equals gain of KE ½mv²; mass cancels, so v = √(2gh) depends only on the height. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Loss of GPE mgh equals gain of KE ½mv²; mass cancels, so v = √(2gh) depends only on the height. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A pendulum of length 1.5 m is pulled aside until the string makes 40° with the vertical and released. Calculate the speed of the bob at the lowest point.
A roller-coaster car starts from rest at the top of a drop of height 12 m. Ignoring friction, calculate its speed at the bottom.
items.markingKey: A. mgh = ½mv² (M1); v = √(2gh) = 15.3 m s⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem:
A spring launcher fires a 0.050 kg ball vertically upwards. The spring is compressed by x and the maximum height h reached by the ball above its release point is measured. Theory (no losses): ½kx² = mgh.

x / m | h / m
0.010 | 0.027
0.015 | 0.058
0.020 | 0.108
0.025 | 0.160
0.030 | 0.242
0.035 | 0.332

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the spring constant k. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±2 %. State k with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) h (y) against x² (x); (b) gradient ≈ 271 m⁻¹; (c) 266 N m⁻¹; (d) (266 ± 5) N m⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) h (y) against x² (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 271 m⁻¹ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) k = 2mg × gradient = 266 N m⁻¹ (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 2 % of the value = 5 N m⁻¹; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: A 60 kg skateboarder starts from rest at the top of a 4.0 m high ramp and descends to the bottom, then rises up a second ramp. (a) Calculate the speed at the bottom assuming no energy losses. (b) At the bottom her actual speed is 7.8 m s⁻¹; calculate the energy dissipated. (c) Determine the maximum height she reaches on the second ramp if the same fraction of energy is lost on the way up. (d) Discuss the main causes of the energy loss.
items.answer: (a) √(2 × 9.81 × 4.0) = 8.86 m s⁻¹; (b) 2354 J − ½ × 60 × 7.8² = 2354 − 1825 = 529 J; (c) 77.5 % retained each stage: h = 4.0 × 0.775² ≈ 2.4 m; (d) friction in the wheel bearings, rolling resistance and air resistance.
items.markingKey: (a) √(2 × 9.81 × 4.0) = 8.86 m s⁻¹; (b) 2354 J − ½ × 60 × 7.8² = 2354 − 1825 = 529 J; (c) 77.5 % retained each stage: h = 4.0 × 0.775² ≈ 2.4 m; (d) friction in the wheel bearings, rolling resistance and air resistance.

items.stem: A 80 kg bungee jumper falls from a bridge on an elastic cord of unstretched length 15 m and spring constant 120 N m⁻¹. Ignore air resistance and the mass of the cord. (a) Calculate the speed when the cord just becomes taut. (b) Determine the maximum extension of the cord. (c) Show that the maximum speed occurs when the extension is 6.54 m and calculate it. (d) Discuss whether the model is realistic.
items.answer: (a) 17.2 m s⁻¹; (b) 22.0 m; (c) maximum speed where kx = mg: 18.9 m s⁻¹; (d) air resistance and energy losses in the cord reduce the extension; real cords do not obey Hooke’s law exactly.
items.markingKey: (a) √(2gL) (A1). (b) mg(L + x) = ½kx² (M1), solve quadratic (A1). (c) a = 0 when kx = mg (M1), energy equation gives v (A1). (d) R1.

items.stem: Two springs stretched by the same extension, one with twice the spring constant. The stiffer spring stores
items.answer: twice the energy
items.markingKey: D. E = ½kx².

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The energy stored in a mass due to its position in a gravitational field; near Earth ΔE_p = mgΔh"?
items.answer: gravitational potential energy
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of gravitational potential energy.

items.stem: Distinguish between elastic potential energy and gravitational potential energy.
items.answer: GPE is stored due to position in a gravitational field (mgΔh); EPE is stored in the deformation of an elastic material (½kx²). Both can be fully recovered as kinetic energy in ideal systems.
items.markingKey: GPE is stored due to position in a gravitational field (mgΔh); EPE is stored in the deformation of an elastic material (½kx²). Both can be fully recovered as kinetic energy in ideal systems. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Kwame writes: "Energy is used up when a ball rolls to a stop." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Energy is conserved; the kinetic energy is transferred to internal energy of the ball and surface and to sound, i.e. dissipated, not destroyed.
items.markingKey: Energy is conserved; the kinetic energy is transferred to internal energy of the ball and surface and to sound, i.e. dissipated, not destroyed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A teacher in Melbourne asks a class to choose the one correct statement about kinetic, gravitational potential and elastic potential energy; conservation of energy. Which statement should be chosen?
options: Energy is conserved; the kinetic energy is transferred to internal energy of the ball and surface and to sound, i.e. dissipated, not destroyed.
Gravitational potential energy is always mgh.
All the energy released by burning fuel in a power station becomes electrical energy.
Energy is used up when a ball rolls to a stop.
items.answer: Energy is conserved; the kinetic energy is transferred to internal energy of the ball and surface and to sound, i.e. dissipated, not destroyed.
items.markingKey: A. The other options are common misconceptions. Energy is conserved; the kinetic energy is transferred to internal energy of the ball and surface and to sound, i.e. dissipated, not destroyed.

items.stem: A cyclist free-wheels at 10 m s⁻¹ up a hill 4.0 m high. Ignoring resistive forces, calculate the speed at the top.
items.markingKey: ½mu² = ½mv² + mgh (M1); v = √(u² − 2gh) = 4.64 m s⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Pumped-storage hydroelectric schemes are an ideal way to store energy from renewable sources."
items.answer: They are currently the most effective large-scale storage, but geography, environmental cost and losses limit them; batteries and other stores complement them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: large capacity, fast response (seconds to minutes); round-trip efficiency about 75–80 %; long lifetime. Arguments against: need suitable geography with two reservoirs at different heights; large environmental impact on valleys; 20–25 % of energy is lost. Supported judgement: They are currently the most effective large-scale storage, but geography, environmental cost and losses limit them; batteries and other stores complement them. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem:

(a) An object of mass 0.5 kg has momentum 4.0 kg m s⁻¹. Calculate its kinetic energy. [2]

(b) With the help of a specific example, explain where the energy goes when a car brakes to a stop. [3]

(c) Outline one argument for and one against the statement: "Pumped-storage hydroelectric schemes are an ideal way to store energy from renewable sources." [4]
items.answer: (a) 16.0 J (b) Kinetic energy is transferred by the work done by friction in the brakes to internal energy (heating) of the brake discs and pads, and then dissipated to the surroundings. (c) They are currently the most effective large-scale storage, but geography, environmental cost and losses limit them; batteries and other stores complement them.

items.stem: Define the term "P = Fv".
items.answer: The power delivered by a force F acting on an object moving at velocity v in the direction of the force
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the power delivered by a force F acting on an object moving at velocity v in the direction of the force. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between energy and power.
items.answer: Energy is the capacity to do work, measured in joules; power is the rate at which energy is transferred, measured in watts (J s⁻¹).
items.markingKey: Energy is the capacity to do work, measured in joules; power is the rate at which energy is transferred, measured in watts (J s⁻¹). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "A more powerful machine always does more work." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Power is the rate of doing work; a less powerful machine can do the same work if it operates for longer.
items.markingKey: Power is the rate of doing work; a less powerful machine can do the same work if it operates for longer. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A 2.0 kW electric heater in a flat in Seoul runs for 4 hours a day. Calculate the energy transferred per day in joules.
items.markingKey: E = Pt = 2000 W × 14400 s (M1) = 2.88 × 10⁷ J (8 kWh, costing 2.2 at 0.28 per kWh) (A1).

items.stem:
This question is about power and efficiency, including P = Fv.

(a) An electric winch with an efficiency of 40 % lifts a 100 kg load through 15 m in 10 s. Calculate the electrical input power. [2]

(b) Explain why a car has a maximum speed on a level road even with the accelerator fully pressed. [3]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "Electric cars are more efficient than petrol cars, so they always produce lower carbon emissions." [4]
items.answer: (a) 3680 W (b) Drag increases with speed while the maximum engine power is fixed; at top speed the driving force P/v equals the resistive force, so the resultant force and acceleration are zero. (c) They are more efficient at the point of use, and usually lower in lifetime emissions, but the advantage depends strongly on the electricity mix and battery production.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Useful P = mgh/t = 1470 W (M1); input = useful/efficiency = 3680 W (A1). (b) [3 marks] Drag increases with speed while the maximum engine power is fixed; at top speed the driving force P/v equals the resistive force, so the resultant force and acceleration are zero. (c) [4 marks] For: electric motors are ~90 % efficient against ~25–30 % for petrol engines; regenerative braking recovers energy; no tailpipe emissions. Against: emissions depend on how the electricity is generated (coal-heavy grids); battery manufacture has a significant carbon footprint; transmission and charging losses. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: They are more efficient at the point of use, and usually lower in lifetime emissions, but the advantage depends strongly on the electricity mix and battery production.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The rate of doing work or transferring energy, P = ΔW/Δt, measured in watts"?
items.answer: power
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of power.

items.stem: Explain why LED lamps are replacing filament lamps.
items.answer: For the same light output LEDs need far less input power because they have a much higher efficiency (less energy dissipated as internal energy), reducing energy cost and emissions.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: For the same light output LEDs need far less input power because they have a much higher efficiency (less energy dissipated as internal energy), reducing energy cost and emissions. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A motor has an efficiency of 80 %. For every 100 J of electrical energy supplied,
options: 20 J is dissipated, mainly as internal energy
20 J of useful work is done
100 J of useful work is done
items.answer: 20 J is dissipated, mainly as internal energy
items.markingKey: A. Useful = 80 J.

options: A kWh is a unit of energy (1 kW for 1 h = 3.6 MJ), used for electricity bills.
Only the component of force along the displacement does work; a centripetal force, for example, is perpendicular to the motion and does no work.
A more powerful machine always does more work.

items.answer: A more powerful machine always does more work.

items.markingKey: D. Useful P = mgh/t = 2450 W (M1); input = useful/efficiency = 4460 W (A1).

items.stem: A kettle rated at 2000 W delivers 1700 W of useful power. Calculate its efficiency as a percentage.
items.markingKey: Efficiency = useful/total × 100 (M1) = 85.0 % (A1).

items.stem: An electric motor in a building lift raises a 900 kg car with passengers through 36 m in 24 s at constant speed. The motor draws 21 kW of electrical power. (a) Calculate the useful power output. (b) Calculate the efficiency. (c) Calculate the energy dissipated in the trip. (d) Suggest two ways the lift system could be made more efficient.
items.answer: (a) P = mgh/t = 900 × 9.81 × 36/24 = 13.2 kW; (b) 13.2/21 = 63 %; (c) (21 − 13.2) × 24 = 186 kJ; (d) use a counterweight; regenerative drives; lubricate/low-friction bearings; lighter cars.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Sankey diagram"?

The energy transferred by a 1 kW device in one hour, 3.6 × 10⁶ J
A flow diagram in which the widths of the arrows are proportional to the amounts of energy transferred
A fuel formed from the remains of ancient organisms, such as coal, oil and natural gas

items.stem: Distinguish between specific energy and energy density.
items.answer: Specific energy is energy per unit mass (J kg⁻¹); energy density is energy per unit volume (J m⁻³). A fuel can be high in one and low in the other, e.g. hydrogen.
items.markingKey: Specific energy is energy per unit mass (J kg⁻¹); energy density is energy per unit volume (J m⁻³). A fuel can be high in one and low in the other, e.g. hydrogen. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A 800 MW power station near Accra burns wood (specific energy 16 MJ kg⁻¹) with an overall efficiency of 40 %. Calculate the mass of fuel burned each second.
items.answer: 125 kg s⁻¹

items.stem: A student claims: "A fuel with a high specific energy must also have a high energy density." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Energy density = specific energy × density; hydrogen has a very high specific energy but, being very low in density, a low energy density.
items.markingKey: Energy density = specific energy × density; hydrogen has a very high specific energy but, being very low in density, a low energy density. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

(a) A petrol engine of efficiency 25 % must deliver 800 MJ of useful work on a journey. Petrol has a specific energy of 46 MJ kg⁻¹. Calculate the mass of petrol needed. [2]

(b) Explain the difference between specific energy and energy density. [4]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "Hydrogen is the ideal fuel of the future." [4]
items.answer: (a) 69.6 kg (b) Specific energy is energy per unit mass (J kg⁻¹); energy density is energy per unit volume (J m⁻³). A fuel can be high in one and low in the other, e.g. hydrogen. (c) Hydrogen is promising where it can be made with renewable electricity, but storage, production and infrastructure problems mean it will complement rather than replace other energy carriers.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Energy input = 800/0.25 MJ (M1); m = 3200/46 = 69.6 kg (A1). (b) [4 marks] Specific energy is energy per unit mass (J kg⁻¹); energy density is energy per unit volume (J m⁻³). A fuel can be high in one and low in the other, e.g. hydrogen. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Hydrogen is promising where it can be made with renewable electricity, but storage, production and infrastructure problems mean it will complement rather than replace other energy carriers.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The energy released per unit mass of a fuel, in J kg⁻¹ (often MJ kg⁻¹)"?
items.answer: specific energy
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of specific energy.

items.stem: Explain why liquid fuels such as petrol and kerosene remain the dominant fuels for aviation.
items.answer: Aircraft are limited by both mass and volume; petrol/kerosene combine a high specific energy (~43–46 MJ kg⁻¹) with a high energy density (~35 MJ L⁻¹), unlike batteries or hydrogen.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Aircraft are limited by both mass and volume; petrol/kerosene combine a high specific energy (~43–46 MJ kg⁻¹) with a high energy density (~35 MJ L⁻¹), unlike batteries or hydrogen. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Mateo and a classmate in Bogotá disagree about energy density of fuels. Which statement is correct?
options: A more powerful machine always does more work.
A fuel with a high specific energy must also have a high energy density.
Typical efficiencies are 35–55 %; most energy is transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy in cooling towers and flue gases.
A heavier object dropped from the same height lands with greater speed.
items.answer: Typical efficiencies are 35–55 %; most energy is transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy in cooling towers and flue gases.
items.markingKey: C. The other options are common misconceptions. Typical efficiencies are 35–55 %; most energy is transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy in cooling towers and flue gases.

items.stem: A car’s tank holds 60 L of ethanol, which has an energy density of 24 MJ L⁻¹. Calculate the chemical energy stored in a full tank.
items.markingKey: C. E = V × energy density = 60 × 24 MJ (M1) = 1.44 × 10⁹ J (A1).

items.stem: Chloé writes: "All the energy released by burning fuel in a power station becomes electrical energy." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Typical efficiencies are 35–55 %; most energy is transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy in cooling towers and flue gases.
items.markingKey: Typical efficiencies are 35–55 %; most energy is transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy in cooling towers and flue gases. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A gas-fired power station has an output of 800 MW and an overall efficiency of 50 %. Natural gas has a specific energy of 55 MJ kg⁻¹ and a density of 0.72 kg m⁻³. (a) Calculate the input power. (b) Calculate the mass of gas burned per second. (c) Calculate the volume of gas burned per second. (d) Draw a labelled Sankey diagram for the station.
items.answer: (a) 1600 MW; (b) 1.6 × 10⁹/5.5 × 10⁷ = 29.1 kg s⁻¹; (c) 29.1/0.72 = 40.4 m³ s⁻¹; (d) input 1600 MW, 800 MW electrical, 800 MW thermal energy to surroundings (arrow widths equal).

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "gravitational potential energy".
items.answer: The energy stored in a mass due to its position in a gravitational field; near Earth ΔE_p = mgΔh
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the energy stored in a mass due to its position in a gravitational field; near Earth ΔE_p = mgΔh. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Define the term "work–energy principle".
items.answer: The work done by the resultant force on an object equals its change in kinetic energy
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the work done by the resultant force on an object equals its change in kinetic energy. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student in Accra is checking notes on kinetic, gravitational potential and elastic potential energy; conservation of energy. Which statement is incorrect?
options: A heavier object dropped from the same height lands with greater speed.

items.answer: A heavier object dropped from the same height lands with greater speed.

items.stem: Explain how the work done in stretching a spring can be found from a force–extension graph.
items.answer: Work is the area under the force–displacement graph; for a spring obeying Hooke’s law it is a triangle of area ½Fx = ½kx².

items.stem: A student claims: "Any force acting on a moving object does work on it." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.

items.stem:
This question is about kinetic, gravitational potential and elastic potential energy; conservation of energy.

(a) A cyclist free-wheels at 12 m s⁻¹ up a hill 4.0 m high. Ignoring resistive forces, calculate the speed at the top. [2]

(b) Explain why the speed of a pendulum bob at the bottom of its swing does not depend on its mass. [3]

(c) Outline one argument for and one against the statement: "Pumped-storage hydroelectric schemes are an ideal way to store energy from renewable sources." [4]
items.answer: (a) 8.09 m s⁻¹ (b) Loss of GPE mgh equals gain of KE ½mv²; mass cancels, so v = √(2gh) depends only on the height. (c) They are currently the most effective large-scale storage, but geography, environmental cost and losses limit them; batteries and other stores complement them.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] ½mu² = ½mv² + mgh (M1); v = √(u² − 2gh) = 8.09 m s⁻¹ (A1). (b) [3 marks] Loss of GPE mgh equals gain of KE ½mv²; mass cancels, so v = √(2gh) depends only on the height. (c) [4 marks] For: large capacity, fast response (seconds to minutes); round-trip efficiency about 75–80 %; long lifetime. Against: need suitable geography with two reservoirs at different heights; large environmental impact on valleys; 20–25 % of energy is lost. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: They are currently the most effective large-scale storage, but geography, environmental cost and losses limit them; batteries and other stores complement them.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The work–energy principle makes Newton’s second law unnecessary."
items.answer: The two approaches complement each other: energy methods are convenient when time is not needed, but Newton’s laws are more fundamental and give more detail.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it solves many problems faster (no time or directions needed); it handles varying forces via the area under graphs. Arguments against: it gives no information about time or direction of motion; it is itself derived from Newton’s second law; friction and internal energy must be accounted for carefully. Supported judgement: The two approaches complement each other: energy methods are convenient when time is not needed, but Newton’s laws are more fundamental and give more detail. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: A 1200 kg car with a maximum power output of 60 kW climbs a steady hill inclined at 5° to the horizontal. The resistive forces total 500 N. items.stem: "Nuclear power is the best way to reduce carbon emissions from electricity generation." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Nuclear can provide large amounts of low-carbon power, but cost, waste and public acceptance mean it is one part of a mix with renewables and storage.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: very high specific energy of uranium means little fuel; low lifecycle CO₂ emissions; reliable baseload output. Arguments against: long-lived radioactive waste; high construction costs and long build times; public concern after accidents (Chernobyl, Fukushima). items.stem: Explain the difference between energy density and specific energy.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a bouncing ball rises to a lower height after each bounce.
items.answer: At each bounce some kinetic energy is transferred to internal energy and sound (inelastic deformation), so less is available to convert back into GPE.

No work is done on the box
items.answer: The work done by gravity equals the work done against friction
items.markingKey: B. ΔKE = 0, so the total work is zero.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a car has a maximum speed on a level road even with the accelerator fully pressed.
items.answer: Drag increases with speed while the maximum engine power is fixed; at top speed the driving force P/v equals the resistive force, so the resultant force and acceleration are zero.

items.answer: A fuel with a high specific energy must also have a high energy density.
